title: OLC’s 1981 defense of presidential regulatory review
shortTitle: OLC’s 1981 defense of presidential regulatory review
summary: OLC defended centralized regulatory review while preserving statutory agency authority and restricting cost-benefit directives to what law permits.
notes:
The 1981 Office of Legal Counsel memorandum defended Executive Order 12,291 as an exercise of presidential supervision under Article II. It argued that nationally accountable presidential oversight could coordinate the administration of numerous statutes and that assigning rulemaking power to a subordinate official does not, without more, prohibit supervision. The historical introduction explains the later continuity and revision of this system under Executive Order 12,866 and the role of OMB’s Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs.

OLC separated procedural analysis from substantive decision. Requiring a regulatory impact analysis could inform an agency’s judgment, while requiring cost-benefit balancing was permissible only when the agency’s statute allowed those considerations. The memorandum assigned calculation and ultimate statutory judgment to the agency head. OMB could question factual claims and methods, request responses, and cause temporary deferral for consultation, but the stated legal theory did not let OMB displace an agency’s lawful ultimate judgment. That qualification is central to the argument’s fit with Youngstown.

The editors reveal a distinction between the published memorandum and earlier internal advice about independent agencies. The earlier advice contemplated procedural supervision while recognizing statutory insulation of substantive discretion. The final Reagan order excluded independent agencies; Clinton later included them in a unified agenda while leaving ordinary mandatory review of their impact analyses outside that framework. The Paperwork Reduction Act separately allows specified independent agencies to override OMB information-collection disapprovals by majority vote. The reading identifies scholarly disagreement about the review system and possible significance of later congressional recognition. These descriptions state the assigned historical treatment and do not claim that the same orders govern unchanged today.
